items.title: What 'Avengers: Endgame' Encore Actually Adds to the Original Movie
items.summary: The energy around Avengers: Doomsday is palpable. Everyone is strapping in and getting ready for Marvel's ultimate multiverse experiment. But apparently, to really get the movie, you have to watch the new version of Avengers: Endgame, called "Encore." Now, cynics will tell you it's just a way to add to their massive box office, and they're probably at least a little right. But Marvel and Disney say this version includes additional scenes to contextualize what you see in Endgame. The gist is that Encore alters the movie's ending and adds three post-credits scenes that set up Avengers: Doomsday. So, what happens in those scenes? We have all the info for you. - YouTubewww.youtube.com Encore Has New Tech Before we get into the story, I thought it was worth mentioning that the Encore also updated some of the tech, so you're watching the best and clearest version of the film to date. Color saturation and contrast across the final battle sequence at the Avengers Compound have been overhauled. Theatrical releases feature optimized Dolby audio mixing and brightness targets specifically tailored for Premium Large Format (PLF) screens, including Infinity Vision. Now, let's talk about the new scenes. Steve & Peggy’s Interrupted Dance In the original 2019 version of the film, we have this peaceful ending where Steve Rogers and Peggy Carter share their very long-awaited dance in their home before fading to black. This is after Steven went back in time to return the stone and then stayed there. But in Encore, the scene continues past the kiss... In Encore, as they dance, there's a sudden knock at the door. Steve cautiously steps out of sight while Peggy opens the door. Standing on the porch is Loki in his TVA uniform, who responds: "I can help you. Both of you." Then, Steve emerges from the shadows to face his former foe before the screen cuts to black. Three Post-Credits Sequences Revealed Marvel is famous for its post-credits scenes. items.title: Hollyland’s New Lark M3 Wireless Mic System Aims to Bring a New Level of Flexibility for Your Audio
items.summary: If you’re looking to record audio for your video projects, you have a lot of options these days. If you’re recording audio for other video-adjacent projects like podcasts, live streams, or other avenues, there are still plenty of options, but you might need a more specific solution. Hollyland has introduced its new Lark M3 wireless microphone system, designed to be flexible for all types of projects, and it looks like a solid follow-up to a popular series that adds more sophistication while staying reliable for basic needs. Let’s look at the Hollyland Lark M3 wireless microphone system, its 32-bit float audio and noise-cancellation features, and everything else it should have to offer. The Hollyland Lark M3 Wireless Microphone System Designed for video crews capturing audio from interviews, multi-person shoots, or other complex production setups, the Hollyland Lark M3 Wireless Microphone System should be versatile enough for a wide range of recording needs. As far as recording specs and features go, the Lark M3 will be able to deliver 48 kHz / 32-bit float recording on iOS devices and 24-bit recording on Android. The system will feature a70 dB signal-to-noise ratio and 125 dB maximum SPL, which should help it be able to record everything from quiet speech to powerful peaks. This new system should also be quite fast, as it will be able to provide 50% faster transmission to carry more audio data, and it will also feature some new AI noise cancellation with deep learning and computational auditory scene analysis technology that should help to suppress transient and continuous background sounds. Price and Availability Available in multiple combo versions, the Lark M3 platform supports up to four transmitters and four receivers, with one receiver able to connect to up to four transmitters and one transmitter able to pair with up to four receivers simultaneously. items.title: Adobe Announces That Its Premiere Mobile App Will Finally Be Available on Android
items.summary: Launched almost exactly a year ago for iPhone creators, the Adobe Premiere mobile app has a long history and several different iterations and names. However, for video editors and content creators who want to edit directly on their favorite smartphone, the Adobe Premiere mobile app is the new home for the widest array of familiar Adobe Premiere tools, including many of the new AI-powered and enhanced ones. For Android owners and shooters, this should be good news, and it follows a pattern seen with other apps like Blackmagic Camera, where iOS versions came out first, and Android took a bit longer than expected. But it’s here, so let’s check it out. Adobe Premiere Mobile App for Android Designed to bring the same intuitive controls and powerful editing features to even more creators than before, the Adobe Premiere mobile app has proven a popular option for video editors familiar with Premiere, as well as the new generation of content creators who may be more familiar with smartphone creation and editing. Regardless of your background, if you’re an Android shooter and editor, the Adobe Premiere mobile app for Android offers a wide range of editing tools centered on a multi-track timeline and frame-accurate editing. Here’s a partial list of some of the tools and features Adobe Premiere mobile app for Android will offer: Getting clearer, studio-quality sound with Enhance Audio. Layering video, music, voiceovers, and effects on an intuitive multi-track timeline. Jumpstarting edits with creator-made templates, or customize your own. Making content stand out with effects, transitions, creative assets, and music from Adobe Stock, your own files, or extracted audio. Editing and exporting videos up to 4K. Creating and editing without a forced login or upgrade prompts. Generating unique assets and pushing your ideas even further with Firefly-powered generative AI features such as Generative Fill, Image-to-Video and Generate Sound Effects. items.title: Editing the Travel Mockumentary 'Conan O’Brien Must Go' With Lead Editor Matthew Shaw
items.summary: Conan O’Brien Must Go is a travel show following Conan O’Brien as he traverses around the world to meet fans from his podcast, “Conan O’Brien Needs a Fan.” Conan’s adventures capture a mix of cultural immersion and comedic absurdity. The production team began each day with dozens of ideas for segments, slowly paring down the number and landing on bits that involved monkeys in a phone store or the host himself stranded on a remote island. As both an editor and a producer, Shaw worked with the production teams in each country for about a week at a time, editing on a rapid schedule that began during shooting. With a comedian like Conan who constantly improvises and episodes that change course in a moment, Shaw gained firsthand insight into how and why they shot each adventure, bit, and joke, which provided valuable context as he edited. Using Adobe Premiere and Frame.io for their flexibility, Shaw saved time by editing dailies and building out his timeline as the team captured footage, letting him adapt quickly and easily to on-the-fly changes. He also relied on Speech-to-Text to pin down specific lines within all of the improv. Below, Shaw takes us inside the process of editing a show built around a host as bold as Conan. How did you become involved in Conan O’Brien Must Go? Matthew Shaw: The majority of my career has been anchored in Conan’s orbit, so when they approached me about leading this show in post, it felt natural. I get to keep making fun, dumb comedies with a group of people I absolutely love, so it was a no-brainer to sign on. Going into a new season and new adventures on this show, how did you prepare your workspace to edit on a short timeline? MS: In our initial talks, we had to figure out how this version would differ from when we made Conan Without Borders (TBS). items.title: Should You Still Move to LA to Make Movies?
items.summary: You know the age-old story of the Hollywood hopeful hopping on a bus somewhere in the Midwest and making the big move to the city of stars, Los Angeles, where movies and dreams are made! At one point, everyone did it—actors, musicians, writers, directors, and other artists of all kinds. At some point, many of us as aspiring filmmakers will make this trek. But is it necessary these days? I ask for a couple of reasons. Today we found Wade Patterson's interview with Film Courage about the move-to-LA dream. Patterson grew up in Jackson, Mississippi, and moved to LA in 2017. He now works as a freelance DP, camera operator, and gaffer while developing his own feature, Death Cipher. I also got a recent question from someone in another part of the world wondering about being a filmmaker and how to break in, so the video feels prescient. Let's dive in. - YouTube www.youtube.com Take That $50 Gig I remember the first time I had my creative writing published anywhere. It was a short story in a magazine. I used the money to buy a satellite navigation system so I could move to LA. It wasn't a ton of money, but by gum, I was published, and I was on my way. Patterson's first paid gig earned him about 50 bucks, and he was grateful for it. "I will say at that time, though, there was also a lot of opportunity to just jump on these really small sets and do, like, super low-budget," he said. "I was working on these super low-budget short films and web series … I think the one rule I have for myself is I don't care what I get paid as long as I get paid something. I think my first gig I made like 50 bucks or something. It was very low." What mattered to him more at that point was meeting people and getting a foot in the door. It was hard for him. It used to be that internships were the way in, and often we were working for free in exchange for "experience." That's thankfully changed, for the most part, now. items.title: Iconic Film Character Intros: How 'Casablanca' Teaches Us to Reveal a Protagonist
items.summary: If I were voting for the best movies of all time, you'd better believe that Casablanca would be on my ballot. It's one of those rare films that gets more perfect every time you watch it. You're on the edge of your seat rooting for both love and revenge and righteous justice the whole time. And the ending still gives me chills. The movie is perhaps the best example of screenwriting I have ever seen, with different writers contributing lines at different times to build something that truly turned out great. You can study the Casablanca screenplay and learn many lessons, but today I want to talk about how it introduced Rick Blaine (Humphrey Bogart) and why every filmmaker should study this scene. Let's dive in. - YouTube www.youtube.com Build the Myth Before the Man What this movie does so well is that it builds our expectations of who Rick is before introducing him, so we're on the edge of our seats with anticipation. We're inside his bar, Rick’s Café Américain, for a very long time before we even glimpse him. We hear his name spoken in hushed tones by refugees, gamblers, and corrupt officials. We even know a few things about him.. "He won't drink with guests." "He never accepts checks." But we take time getting to the man because director Michael Curtiz built high expectations in the audience's mind. When a camera finally cuts to the man himself, the audience is already primed to pay attention and to embrace the star power of Humphrey Bogart as this legend as well. - YouTube www.youtube.com The Anatomy of the Reveal When Curtiz finally brings us into Rick’s presence, we get glimpses of his body before we reveal the person. He's signing a piece of paper when we meet him. The camera doesn't start on Bogart’s face. It opens on a close-up of a check authorization. We immediately see his authority and economic power within this ecosystem. He's totally in charge here. The next thing we notice about Rick is that he is totally alone. items.title: Film Quote of the Day: The Morgan Freeman Line From The 1995 Thriller That Redefined Movie Endings
items.summary: I just got Se7en in ultra 4K, and I've been loving those sumptuous David Fincher frames that take you into one of the darkest murder stories ever. We've talked about how the moral of Se7en is that evil wins. And today, I want to cover some of the dialogue that explicitly states that argument, snuck into the movie by the great Andrew Kevin Walker. All of this is contained in a line delivered by Morgan Freeman’s weary Detective William Somerset. One that closes the movie and sums up everything we've seen up until that point. Let's dive in. - YouTubewww.youtube.com The Scene in Question Up until the final moments, Se7en feels like a slow march into pitch-black darkness. You keep thinking they're going to catch this murderer and that everything is going to be okay. I mean, we've grown to love Detectives Somerset and Mills (Brad Pitt). They have given everything, having spent the entire film chasing John Doe (Kevin Spacey), only for him to give himself up. He shows up covered in blood, and that's when the dread hits you...whose blood is it? John Doe leads our detectives into the middle of the desert, where a cardboard box is delivered, one that turns all the events we've seen before into a plot with a payoff. That's when John Doe’s sick plan reaches its horrifying completion, and we hear "What's in the box?" While that may be the movie's famous quote, what comes next is the heart. Mills breaks, pulls the trigger, and becomes the final piece of Doe's twisted puzzle. But as Mills is driven away in the back of a police cruiser, the camera lingers on Somerset. And he talks over the final scenes of the movie, reconciling everything that's happened at the same time as the audience. “Ernest Hemingway once wrote, ‘The world is a fine place and worth fighting for.’ I agree with the second part.” - YouTubewww.youtube.com What The Quote Means We've spent all the time watching this movie hoping for a happy ending. items.title: SatOV: Restoring Spatial Priors for Training-Free Open-Vocabulary Segmentation in Remote Sensing Imagery
items.summary: arXiv:2609.22834v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Open-vocabulary semantic segmentation (OVS) of remote sensing imagery is a challenging pixel-level task requiring strong generalization and adaptation to the spatial characteristics of remote sensing data. Although existing vision-language foundation models perform well in general domains, their image-level classification design weakens the spatial priors needed for high-resolution remote sensing segmentation: structural spatial relations are degraded during deep feature transformation, and fine-grained spatial details are lost during downsampling. To address these complementary deficiencies, we propose SatOV, a training-free framework for open-vocabulary remote sensing segmentation that restores spatial priors at two stages of the representation pipeline. Specifically, Residual QQ Attention (ResQQ) extracts Query-Key self-attention from an intermediate CLIP layer and fuses it with final-layer Query-Query attention via a residual combination, restoring structural spatial priors suppressed by the final-layer representation. Spatially Modulated Upsampling (SatUp) uses the original high-resolution RGB image as spatial guidance, combining spatial feature modulation with guided cross-attention to reconstruct pixel-level textures and boundaries. Extensive experiments on DOTA, UDD, LoveDA, and Vaihingen show that SatOV consistently improves training-free OVS and achieves competitive quantitative and qualitative results against state-of-the-art methods. These results validate the effectiveness of restoring spatial priors at both the representation and spatial-resolution stages for remote sensing open-vocabulary segmentation.

items.title: AniPrO: Interpretable Anime Image Provenance Detection via Multi-Dimensional Semantic Reasoning
items.summary: arXiv:2609.23345v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As generative AI becomes increasingly used in anime-style image creation, distinguishing human-drawn, AI-inpainted, and text-to-image images is important for copyright attribution, visual provenance, and content governance. Existing AI-generated image detectors mainly target real-world photographs and often overlook anime-specific cues such as flat coloring, exaggerated structures, and artistic line control. To address this gap, we propose AniPrO, a multi-dimensional description-enhanced framework for interpretable anime image provenance. Built upon AnimeDL-2M, AniPrO contains 15,000 balanced samples from a 35,000-image candidate pool, covering Real, Inpainting, and Text2Image categories with structured five-dimensional descriptions. We further introduce AniPrO-SFD-Bench and AniPrO-MFR-Bench to evaluate provenance detection from statistical feature discrimination and multimodal fusion reasoning perspectives. Experiments show that structured semantic guidance reveals systematic AI-generation biases, such as the gap between global visual plausibility and local detail coherence, and improves the detection of challenging inpainting samples. The dataset and code will be released at: https://github.com/YAN-LIU05/AniPrO.

Built upon AnimeDL-2M, AniPrO contains 15,000 balanced samples from a 35,000-image candidate pool, covering Real, Inpainting, and Text2Image categories with structured five-dimensional descriptions. We further introduce AniPrO-SFD-Bench and AniPrO-MFR-Bench to evaluate provenance detection from statistical feature discrimination and multimodal fusion reasoning perspectives. Experiments show that structured semantic guidance reveals systematic AI-generation biases, such as the gap between global visual plausibility and local detail coherence, and improves the detection of challenging inpainting samples. items.title: CoaG: Cylinders on a Grid: Coarse 3D Layout Control for Video Generation
items.summary: arXiv:2609.24208v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We ask how little geometry a person has to draw to control both where people stand and where the camera moves in a generated video. Our answer is a ground plane and one cylinder per person. A user draws a grid on the ground, places one cylinder where each person should stand, moves the cylinders and the camera over 81 frames, and the model renders a photoreal video in which the people occupy the cylinders' positions, move as the cylinders move, and are seen from the drawn camera. Appearance comes from a text prompt and a background reference image; layout and motion come from the geometry. Because no dataset pairs such a signal with video, we build the pairs ourselves: an automatic engine writes 2000 captions from a combinatorial seed, generates a clip for each with a text-to-video model, and lifts every clip back to its geometry with person tracking, background inpainting, an agentic ground-mask loop, feed-forward multi-view reconstruction and a plane fit, with no real footage and no manual labels. A LoRA on Wan2.2-Fun-Control trained on 1935 such tuples follows drawn layouts and camera paths on hold-out clips: the generated people match the cylinders' count, order, position and height, the text changes who they are, the reference image changes where they are, and dolly-in, orbit, pan and crane paths are followed, dolly-out only weakly.

items.title: Terror-ific! Fantastic Fest Announces its 2026 Award-Winning Films and Pitches
items.summary: Despite it still being blistering hot and sunny on the patio deck at the Alamo Drafthouse on South Lamar in Austin, Texas, you’d be surprised to learn that Fantastic Fest, the annual genre film festival that serves as a de facto kick-off to the cool and spooky horror season, is now complete. As Fantastic Fest wraps up its final days, the big winners of the Fantastic Fest 2026 awards have been announced, including some terror-ific, inspiring shorts, features, and pitches worth checking out. (Who knows, as we discuss in our Fantastic Fest pod coverage, any of these films or projects might be the next Obsession, the next Backrooms, or the next horror sensation to sweep the nation.) Let’s check out the award-winning films from this year’s Fantastic Fest. Fantastic Fest 2026 Awards Despite the heat, the theaters at the Alamo Drafthouse in Austin were cold, dark, and as rambunctious as always, with fans and industry insiders from across the globe converging to watch, celebrate, and party with their horror (and other genre-loving) film brethren. This year’s fest was no different, featuring a diverse array of genre films that ranged widely in terms of locals, gimmicks, and plenty of ingenious kills. “Our winning films embody distinctive and powerful voices from a wide range of cultures, and the exciting new generation of talent shaping the future of genre cinema. It is our privilege to give these exciting filmmakers the platform and recognition they deserve, and we are so grateful for our jurors to help us celebrate the very best in genre filmmaking.” - Director of Programming Annick Mahnert. items.title: Adobe’s Acquisition of Topaz Labs is Complete as Double Down on AI Enhancements Continues
items.summary: The AI double down continues as companies in the film and video space are pushing more and more chips into the pot. The latest AI double down comes from Adobe, which has announced that its acquisition of Topaz Labs (which we covered when it was first announced) is now complete. With the deal now complete, the company says Topaz Labs will continue to operate as a standalone brand, but Adobe plans to bring its advanced capabilities directly into its creative tools and workflows, including Adobe Firefly, Photoshop, Premiere, and likely more. Now that it’s complete, here’s what we know so far about what this acquisition means for Adobe and the doubled-down AI future. Adobe Acquires Topaz Labs As we covered when the deal was first announced, this is a pretty big acquisition for Adobe, at least in terms of its full embrace of AI video and image enhancement models and tools. It’s not the only AI news, of course, but it’s another brick in the new building that Adobe is building that is becoming more AI-aided and integrated. Adobe isn't the only major player in film, video, and other creative services doubling down. We’ve seen Blackmagic Design’s DaVinci Resolve add new AI assistant integration recently, and countless other new AI apps, tools, and features across all areas of production. What’s perhaps most interesting is that, with this deal now complete, Adobe has already added Topaz Labs technology directly into Adobe Firefly and Photoshop, where users can enhance their images and videos while preserving the natural look and detail of the original. The company’s proprietary Neurostream technology can also let creatives run complex AI models on their own devices or use Topaz Labs' cloud-based option. items.title: The 'Jaws' Sequel Tagline So Bad It Became Iconic for the Wrong Reasons
items.summary: Some movies just don't need a sequel. I think most people would agree that Jaws is one of them. You probably already know that Jaws was Steven Spielberg's first major hit and the spark for the summer blockbuster era. Its story of a small beach community welcoming summer tourists and a deadly great white shark is one of the best creature features ever put to screen, mostly because the characters are so good. You've got the fearful sheriff, the nerdy academic, and the salty seafarer, and all of them are well-developed, fun people to watch. Spoiler, but they kill that shark. So a sequel doesn't really make sense. But somehow we get to 1987 and a fourth movie, Jaws: The Revenge. In this one, Ellen Brody (returning star Lorraine Gary) becomes convinced that a great white is stalking and hunting her family across the ocean to avenge the sharks killed in previous films. The film co-stars Michael Caine as an airplane pilot. Caine famously missed collecting his Academy Award for Hannah and Her Sisters because he was busy filming this movie, later saying, "I have never seen the film, but by all accounts it is terrible. However, I have seen the house that it built, and it is terrific." The film was not a success. It's currently sitting at a 2% on Rotten Tomatoes, so it's safe to say it was a critical disaster. However, the tagline is one of the most recognizable pieces of movie marketing ever written. Today we want to look at the film… and how to sell something you've made. - YouTube www.youtube.com This Time… It's Personal A lot about this film is confusing. It's the last of the Jaws movies, but it takes place after Jaws 2 and ignores Jaws 3-D entirely. It features a now-widowed Ellen Brody, mostly because Roy Scheider declined to play Chief Brody again. The production was harried and plagued by difficulties. And the project moved wildly fast.
